paragraphs: A*Net tackles a scaling problem in knowledge graph reasoning: following paths through a graph can support reasoning beyond learned entity embeddings, but the number of possible paths grows exponentially. This makes path exploration expensive in both memory and computation, helping explain why embedding methods have dominated reasoning on large knowledge graphs.

Inspired by the A* shortest-path algorithm, the method learns a priority function that selects important nodes and edges at each iteration. Training and inference therefore concentrate on a chosen portion of the graph. The selection ratios are adjustable, giving users a direct way to trade reasoning performance against computational efficiency.

On benchmarks covering both transductive and inductive reasoning, A*Net remains competitive with leading path-based approaches while visiting only 10% of nodes and edges per iteration. On the million-scale ogbl-wikikg2 dataset, it reports a new state-of-the-art result and faster convergence than embedding methods. These findings show that selective exploration can make path-based reasoning workable at a scale previously inaccessible to such methods.
neurips-2023-a-net-a-scalable-path-based.tldr: A*Net learns which graph paths to prioritize, enabling competitive knowledge graph reasoning while exploring far fewer nodes and edges.

paragraphs: Missing data can affect demographic groups differently, making it relevant to both prediction quality and fairness. This paper studies the common workflow of filling in missing values before training a classifier. Its central concern is that replacing missing entries can erase information carried by the pattern of what was missing.

The authors prove that training on imputed data can substantially worsen the fairness and average accuracy that a classifier can achieve. The mechanism is informational: missingness patterns often help predict the target label, and the imputation step can discard that signal. This is a statement about what can happen, rather than a claim that every use of imputation necessarily produces discrimination.

The proposed scalable algorithms adapt fairness interventions to different missingness patterns while preserving their information. They are designed to work with any existing fairness-intervention algorithm. Across the reported datasets, combining them with state-of-the-art fairness methods consistently improves both fairness and accuracy relative to imputing first and then classifying. The results support treating missingness as part of the learning problem.
neurips-2023-adapting-fairness-intervent.tldr: Preserving information about which values are missing improves the reported fairness and accuracy of classification compared with imputing first.

paragraphs: Simulating adaptive leaky integrate-and-fire neurons involves a familiar compromise. Small time steps capture neural activity more accurately but require many sequential computations. Larger steps reduce computation while sacrificing accuracy. The paper addresses this trade-off by changing how the neuron model is computed, particularly when fine timing resolution is needed.

The authors reinterpret the ALIF model algorithmically to reduce the sequential work involved in simulation. This makes the computation more amenable to parallel execution on GPUs. The goal is to retain small time steps while making training faster, so speed improvements do not have to come from using a coarser simulation.

On synthetic benchmarks, the implementation produces more than a 50-fold training speedup with small time steps. It also achieves performance comparable to standard ALIF implementations on several supervised classification tasks, with substantially shorter training times. Finally, the authors demonstrate fitting real recordings of cortical neurons quickly and accurately. That application highlights the value of retaining sub-millisecond resolution when precise spike timing is central to the task.
neurips-2023-addressing-the-speed-accura.tldr: An algorithmic reformulation makes adaptive spiking-neuron simulations more GPU-parallel, accelerating training while retaining fine time resolution.

paragraphs: Non-line-of-sight imaging reconstructs hidden scenes using measurements that allow a system to see around corners. Collecting spatially dense measurements takes time, so this paper asks whether useful reconstructions can be obtained from much sparser scans. Existing approaches face difficulties with reconstruction quality or the time needed to compute a result.

The proposed network divides the task into measurement recovery and volume reconstruction. First, a transient recovery network extracts and combines features to predict high-resolution measurements from the sparse input. A second network uses the linear physics of light transport to reconstruct the hidden volume. Additional regularization encourages local detail and reduces excessive smoothing.

Experiments on synthetic and public real-world data report superior performance across different scanning grids. The method also shows robustness with an 8-by-8 scanning grid and inference 50 times faster than an existing iterative solution. Together, these results suggest that combining learned measurement recovery with a physical reconstruction model can reduce both scanning demands and reconstruction time in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2023-deep-non-line-of-sight-imag.tldr: A two-stage neural network combines sparse-measurement recovery with light-transport physics to reconstruct hidden scenes quickly.

paragraphs: This paper studies a seller who chooses both a product price and a rule for communicating information about product quality. Before quality is realized, the seller commits to the signals buyers may receive. Bayesian persuasion models how those signals affect buyers' valuations and purchasing decisions, making pricing and information disclosure a joint optimization problem.

The seller initially does not know the demand function and must learn from purchase responses. The authors give a computationally efficient online algorithm with regret O(T^(2/3)(m log T)^(1/3)) when valuation is linear in quality. Here, T counts rounds and m counts possible quality values. Regret measures revenue lost relative to an optimal strategy with advance knowledge.

The guarantee requires monotonicity and Lipschitz assumptions on valuation, but no smoothness or Lipschitz assumption on demand. For constant m, it matches a dynamic-pricing lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Further results for additive valuations include a bound independent of m when m is at most T^(1/3), showing how additional valuation structure can improve the dependence on quality-domain size.
neurips-2023-dynamic-pricing-and-learnin.tldr: An online algorithm jointly learns prices and quality-disclosure strategies with provable revenue-regret bounds under stated valuation assumptions.

paragraphs: McKean-Vlasov equations describe populations of particles affected by drift, diffusion, and collective interactions. Some physically important interactions become unbounded when particles collide, making the equations particularly difficult to solve with theoretical guarantees. The paper considers this challenge, including interactions associated with plasma physics and the vorticity description of two-dimensional fluid flow.

The authors build their approach around entropy dissipation in the underlying system. They derive a potential function that controls the KL divergence between a candidate solution and the true solution. This gives the training objective a mathematical connection to solution error, rather than treating the objective only as a convenient quantity to optimize.

Their Entropy-dissipation Informed Neural Network uses neural networks to approximate the velocity field and minimizes that potential function. Comparisons with state-of-the-art neural solvers across several example problems demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The contribution connects a theoretically motivated measure of discrepancy with a trainable neural representation, offering a promising route for handling equations whose singular interactions make standard solution strategies challenging.
neurips-2023-entropy-dissipation-informe.tldr: EINN trains neural velocity fields using an entropy-based objective that controls solution discrepancy for McKean-Vlasov equations.

paragraphs: A preference judgment about an entire language-model response gives limited guidance about what went wrong within it. This becomes especially restrictive for long answers, where factual mistakes, irrelevant passages, and missing information may coexist. The paper uses more detailed human feedback to turn those separate problems into explicit training signals.

Fine-Grained RLHF makes rewards more specific in two ways. It supplies rewards after individual segments, such as sentences, and uses multiple reward models for different feedback categories. Consequently, training can receive information about both where an issue occurs and what kind of issue it is, instead of relying only on a single judgment of the complete response.

Experiments on detoxification and long-form question answering show improvements supported by automatic measures and human evaluations. The authors also demonstrate that changing the combination of reward models can customize model behavior. The findings indicate that the structure of feedback matters: richer annotations can guide improvements along distinct dimensions and make those dimensions available as controls during language-model training.
neurips-2023-fine-grained-human-feedback.tldr: Segment-level, error-specific human feedback improves language-model training and enables behavior customization through different reward combinations.

paragraphs: Oriented object detection requires predicting boxes that follow an object's rotation. Horizontal bounding boxes are more readily available as training labels, but they provide less direct information about orientation. H2RBox-v2 seeks to narrow the performance gap between detectors trained with these horizontal labels and detectors trained with explicitly rotated boxes.

The method combines a weakly supervised branch with a self-supervised branch that learns orientation from symmetry in visual objects. Consistency under flips and rotations provides additional learning signals. Practical techniques also address issues such as angle periodicity, where different numerical angles can describe equivalent orientations, helping stabilize and improve the detector.

The reported results are close to those of Rotated FCOS trained with rotation annotations across DOTA, HRSC, and FAIR1M. H2RBox-v2 exceeds that counterpart on some reported results and falls below it on others. It is also less susceptible than H2RBox to poor annotations and limited training data. These findings support symmetry as a useful source of orientation supervision when the available labels specify only horizontal boxes.
neurips-2023-h2rbox-v2-incorporating-sym.tldr: H2RBox-v2 uses symmetry-based self-supervision to learn rotated object boxes from horizontal annotations with performance close to rotation-supervised detection.

paragraphs: HASSOD learns to detect objects and represent their part-to-whole relationships without human supervision. Its starting point is that recognizing objects involves more than identifying separate regions: an image can contain meaningful structures at several levels of composition. The method uses that hierarchy as an additional source of learning information.

It groups image regions into object masks through hierarchical adaptive clustering of self-supervised visual representations. The number of objects is determined adaptively for each image. By examining how masks cover one another, HASSOD constructs trees describing their compositional relationships. Learning these relationships improves detection and makes the resulting structure more interpretable.

The training procedure adapts the Mean Teacher framework instead of using repeated rounds of self-training, producing a smoother and more efficient process. Experiments report improvements over existing self-supervised detection approaches on prevalent image datasets. Mask AR increases from 20.2 to 22.5 on LVIS and from 17.0 to 26.0 on SA-1B. These findings support using automatically discovered composition to strengthen object learning without manual annotations.
neurips-2023-hassod-hierarchical-adaptiv.tldr: HASSOD improves object detection without human labels by learning adaptive object masks and their hierarchical relationships.

paragraphs: In model-based reinforcement learning, an agent learns an environment model and uses it to improve its policy. These two processes interact closely. Updating the model too aggressively can hurt policy performance, even when the update seems helpful for model learning. This paper studies how to account for that interaction during fine-tuning.

The authors identify shortcomings in two existing approaches. Some methods overlook the effect of model shift, while others restrict it using a fixed threshold that can be difficult to adapt throughout training. They derive an optimization objective that jointly accounts for model shift and model bias, then use it to formulate an adaptive model fine-tuning process.

The resulting algorithm, USB-PO, adjusts model updates with a theoretically derived performance-improvement guarantee while avoiding model overfitting. Empirical evaluations report state-of-the-art performance on several challenging benchmark tasks. The contribution is a way to coordinate model revision with policy optimization: the learning objective considers both the model's errors and the consequences of changing the model that policy learning depends on.
neurips-2023-how-to-fine-tune-the-model-.tldr: USB-PO jointly accounts for model bias and model shift to adapt environment-model updates during policy optimization.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when the environment's transition model is unknown and losses can change adversarially between episodes. It assumes that transitions have a low-rank decomposition and that each episode's loss function is fully revealed afterward. This feedback setting gives the learner more information than observing only the losses of its chosen actions.

The proposed policy-optimization algorithm, POLO, interleaves learning a representation, exploring the environment, and exploiting what has been learned. Its regret bound grows as K^(5/6) with the number of episodes, alongside factors involving transition rank, action count, model-class size, and discounting. Because growth in K is sublinear, the bound gives diminishing average regret over sufficiently many episodes.

POLO is oracle-efficient, and its regret guarantee does not depend on the size of the state space, which may be arbitrarily large. A separate lower bound establishes that low-rank MDPs are statistically harder than linear MDPs in this regret setting. Together, the results show both the feasibility of learning under these assumptions and a meaningful difficulty introduced by the broader representation class.
neurips-2023-learning-adversarial-low-ra.tldr: POLO achieves sublinear regret in unknown low-rank environments with adversarial losses and full-information feedback, without state-space-size dependence.

paragraphs: Pretrained models are widely reused for new tasks, but strong predictive performance does not by itself explain how adversarial robustness transfers. This paper examines the relationship between a learned representation and the robustness of a downstream linear predictor. The representation is the intermediate description of inputs on which that predictor relies.

The authors show that the robustness of this underlying representation can constrain downstream robustness regardless of the pretraining protocol. They prove a loss bound that is independent of any particular downstream task and provide a separate criterion for robust classification. These results identify representation-level properties as relevant to what a later linear prediction stage can achieve.

Practical evaluations validate the theoretical findings. The authors also explain how the results can calibrate expectations about downstream robustness and when they are useful for optimal transfer learning. The contribution is an initial characterization of requirements on representations for reliable performance after adaptation. Its stated scope centers on linear downstream predictors, giving a specific setting in which robustness transfer can be analyzed rather than assumed.
neurips-2023-on-transfer-of-adversarial-.tldr: The robustness of pretrained representations can constrain downstream linear predictors, with theoretical bounds and practical validation.

paragraphs: The paper studies online reinforcement learning under the assumption that every policy's action values are linear functions of given state-action features. This setting is broader than linear MDPs, which impose linear structure directly on rewards and transitions. The question is whether the broader setting still permits learning with a manageable number of interactions.

The key observation concerns states where, for any policy, available actions have approximately equal values. Following a fixed policy through these states effectively skips decisions that contribute little value distinction. The authors show that this transformation exposes a linear MDP, and design an algorithm that learns which states to skip while learning within the resulting problem.

They establish the first polynomial-sample-complexity online algorithm for this setting, with an inverse-square dependence on target accuracy in the stated interaction bound. The analysis also covers misspecification, with sample complexity degrading gracefully as representation error increases. However, the algorithm is computationally inefficient. The result therefore establishes interaction efficiency and a structural explanation of learnability, rather than an immediately efficient implementation.
neurips-2023-online-rl-in-linearly-q-pi-.tldr: Learning which nearly action-indifferent states to skip enables sample-efficient online learning under linear action-value realizability, though the algorithm is computationally inefficient.

paragraphs: When a controller cannot observe the full state of a system, it must use past observations to infer what is happening now. A highly flexible history encoder can extract useful information, but it can also overfit to sequences encountered during training. This paper seeks a useful balance between expressiveness and robustness to environmental changes.

The authors draw inspiration from PID controllers, arguing that summing and differencing observations can accumulate the information needed for many control tasks. They propose two history-encoding architectures: one directly incorporates PID features, while the other extends those principles into a form usable across arbitrary control tasks. Both introduce structure into how a learned policy processes time.

Compared with earlier approaches, the resulting policies often perform better and are more robust on tracking tasks. On a suite of locomotion tasks, they achieve 1.7-fold better performance on average than previous state-of-the-art methods. These findings support structured history processing as a useful design choice for partially observable control, with the reported benefits extending beyond the tracking setting that naturally motivates PID-inspired features.
neurips-2023-pid-inspired-inductive-bias.tldr: PID-inspired history encoders improve reported control performance and often robustness when reinforcement-learning policies cannot observe the full system state.

paragraphs: Weight-sharing quantization reduces the number of distinct values used by a neural network, helping reduce inference energy expenditure. This paper argues that deciding which weights should share a value requires attention to their positions in the network. Two weights with similar numerical values need not have the same freedom to change.

The method learns position-specific uncertainty distributions using a Bayesian neural-network framework and a variational relaxation. These distributions guide which cluster centers a weight can move toward and how far it can move. A new initialization and regularization term support training on complex model-and-dataset combinations, while iterative clustering uses the learned flexibility to improve compressibility.

Experiments on ResNets and transformer architectures report better compressibility and accuracy than state-of-the-art methods. For DeiT-Tiny on ImageNet, more than five million weights are represented using 296 unique values, with a reported 1.6% top-1 accuracy improvement over the compared quantization method. The findings support learning how sensitive individual weight positions are before forcing them to share values, rather than grouping weights solely by numerical similarity.
neurips-2023-probabilistic-weight-fixing.tldr: Probabilistic Weight Fixing uses learned, position-specific weight uncertainty to improve neural-network quantization and compressibility.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks commonly exchange information between neighboring nodes, which can restrict their ability to capture global structure. This paper develops a framework connecting discrete graph networks with continuous diffusion objectives. The two-way mapping allows the authors to design objectives in the continuous setting and derive discrete models with mathematical guarantees.

One application addresses over-smoothing, where repeated graph processing makes node representations too alike. The authors link existing layer-by-layer embedding models to an integral involving squared graph gradients. They introduce total variation and a selective mechanism to align diffusion with community structure and improve the trade-off between network depth and over-smoothing.

A second application builds a generative adversarial model for predicting spreading flows through a neural transport equation. Its objective minimizes transportation within communities while maximizing flows between communities to address potentially vanishing flows. The resulting models report state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks including Cora, Citeseer, and Pubmed. The broader contribution is a principled connection between continuous objectives and graph-network design, demonstrated through two distinct learning problems.
neurips-2023-re-think-and-re-design-grap.tldr: A continuous-diffusion framework guides the design of graph networks that address over-smoothing and model spreading flows.

paragraphs: A common explanation for visual-model vulnerability is that models exploit high-frequency image information that people cannot perceive. Approaches motivated by this view often suppress learning from those components. This paper revisits the explanation by defining high-frequency components through the long-tailed distribution observed in image frequency spectra.

Across the tested datasets and network structures, standard training produces strong sensitivity to these components. The authors connect that sensitivity to underfitting, which they attribute to the limited information contained in the high-frequency portion. This interpretation motivates improving how models learn from that information, instead of treating its presence only as a source of vulnerability.

The proposed Balance Spectrum Sampling strategy counteracts the long-tailed frequency distribution and strengthens learning on high-frequency components. When combined with existing defenses, it achieves a substantially better robustness-accuracy trade-off in the reported experiments. The findings indicate that encouraging such learning has potential to improve model performance. They support a more nuanced account of high-frequency information, where insufficient learning can contribute to sensitivity in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2023-revisiting-visual-model-rob.tldr: Balance Spectrum Sampling improves the reported robustness-accuracy trade-off by helping visual models learn underrepresented high-frequency information.

paragraphs: Brain-network studies often combine structural connectivity with functional connectivity to use complementary information. The relationship between these modalities is complex and varies across brain regions. This paper argues that fusion methods should explicitly account for those regional differences, rather than combine representations through a uniform pattern that overlooks how structure and function relate locally.

RH-BrainFS first uses a brain-subgraph module to extract regional characteristics. It then applies a transformer-based fusion bottleneck to address differences between the structural and functional representations. The design places regional information within the fusion process, making heterogeneous relationships between modalities part of what the model is built to handle.

Experiments across a variety of neuroscience tasks report better performance than several state-of-the-art methods. The results support the proposed treatment of regional heterogeneity as useful for multimodal brain-network learning. The main contribution is therefore both a modeling emphasis and an architecture: identify where the relationship between modalities differs, and incorporate those regional characteristics when combining them for downstream prediction.
neurips-2023-rh-brainfs-regional-heterog.tldr: RH-BrainFS improves reported neuroscience-task performance by accounting for regional differences when fusing structural and functional brain networks.

paragraphs: SustainGym addresses a benchmarking gap in reinforcement learning for sustainable energy systems. Without standardized environments, researchers have difficulty tracking progress within an application and identifying the problems that most need attention. The paper contributes a shared evaluation suite intended to make those comparisons and research priorities easier to establish.

The suite contains five environments covering realistic energy-system tasks, including electric-vehicle charging and carbon-aware scheduling of data-center jobs. It evaluates algorithms under realistic distribution shifts and in settings involving multiple agents. These features extend the evaluation beyond performance under a single fixed set of conditions, reflecting challenges relevant to the intended applications.

The authors find that standard, readily available reinforcement-learning algorithms leave substantial room for improvement. This result makes the suite useful as a way to expose weaknesses as well as measure progress. The contribution is a set of demanding sustainability-oriented tests and evidence that existing methods do not yet resolve their challenges, helping frame further work toward applying reinforcement learning in real energy systems.
neurips-2023-sustaingym-reinforcement-le.tldr: SustainGym provides five realistic sustainable-energy benchmarks that reveal substantial room to improve standard reinforcement-learning algorithms.

paragraphs: Autonomous-driving development needs simulations populated by agents that behave realistically and interact with one another. The Waymo Open Sim Agents Challenge focuses on this problem as a public research task. Its goal is to encourage simulators that can support both evaluating driving behavior models and training those models.

The paper introduces the challenge together with metrics and an evaluation methodology. This makes the contribution more than a call to build simulation agents: it also provides a shared way to assess proposed methods. The authors present results for several baseline agent approaches and examine submissions from the competition, giving concrete examples of methods evaluated within that framework.

The paper also discusses open problems, positioning realistic interactive simulation as an ongoing research challenge. Its central contribution is evaluation infrastructure and comparative analysis rather than a single new simulator. By bringing task definition, metrics, baseline results, and competition submissions together, it creates a common setting for studying how well simulated agents support the needs of autonomous-driving research.
neurips-2023-the-waymo-open-sim-agents-c.tldr: WOSAC establishes a public challenge and evaluation framework for realistic, interactive simulation agents in autonomous driving.

paragraphs: As high-quality text becomes harder to scale, repeating existing pretraining data is an obvious way to continue language-model training. This paper empirically investigates what happens when models make multiple passes over the same data. It finds susceptibility to overfitting and degradation across epochs, showing that additional exposure does not automatically yield better results.

The study examines which factors influence that degradation. Dataset size, model parameters, and training objectives have substantial effects, while dataset quality and model FLOPs are less influential in the reported analysis. Most tested regularization techniques provide little improvement. Dropout is a notable exception, although it requires careful tuning as model size increases.

The authors also find that mixture-of-experts models can support cost-effective hyperparameter tuning for computationally expensive dense models with comparable trainable parameter counts. This offers a possible route to reducing the cost of finding useful training settings. Together, the findings clarify both the risks of repeated-data pretraining and the empirical value of carefully tuned dropout when fresh training tokens are constrained.
neurips-2023-to-repeat-or-not-to-repeat-.tldr: Repeated pretraining data can cause degradation, while carefully tuned dropout and mixture-of-experts-based tuning offer useful responses in the reported study.

paragraphs: Serving large models creates substantial computational and latency costs. This paper studies two ways to reduce them together: caching previous queries and choosing which model in an ensemble should process a query. Joint optimization matters because both decisions contribute to the cost of handling the incoming workload.

The authors develop an algorithm with optimal rates in offline and online tabular settings. It combines a learned model selector with either Greedy Dual Size with Frequency or Least Expected Cost caching. The theoretical result concerns these specified settings, establishing how coordinated caching and model choice can reduce inference cost within the analyzed formulation.

Simulations show improvements of up to 50-fold over the baseline when the maximum-to-minimum cost ratio is 100. On real datasets, the reported improvement is 4.3-fold in FLOPs when the FLOPs ratio is 10, and 1.8-fold in latency when the average-latency ratio is 1.85. These conditions give context to the gains and support evaluating caching and model selection as a combined resource-allocation problem.
neurips-2023-towards-optimal-caching-and.tldr: Jointly optimizing caching and model selection achieves optimal rates in tabular settings and substantial reported inference-cost reductions.

paragraphs: This paper develops faster ways to estimate effective resistance between nodes in undirected expander graphs. Its main strategy is to preprocess the graph into a compact sketch, so later queries can be answered quickly without repeating the full computation. The accuracy target is a multiplicative factor of 1 plus or minus epsilon.

For a graph with n nodes and m edges, construction takes roughly m/epsilon time and the sketch uses roughly n/epsilon bits, suppressing logarithmic factors. It supports roughly constant-time pair queries with a high-probability guarantee. The same approach estimates resistance for all edges in roughly m/epsilon time, improving the cited previous runtimes for sparse graphs.

The authors also establish a conditional lower bound for a broad class of algorithms estimating resistance across all node pairs. This distinguishes efficient preprocessing and individual queries from the work required for a complete collection of pairwise estimates. They extend the underlying tools to sketching pseudoinverses of positive semidefinite matrices and estimating eigenvalue functions, connecting the graph results to broader matrix-computation problems.
neurips-2023-towards-optimal-effective-r.tldr: New sketches accelerate effective-resistance estimation on expander graphs, alongside conditional hardness results and extensions to matrix problems.

paragraphs: Applying reinforcement learning to financial trading requires much more than selecting a learning algorithm. A project must connect data collection, feature engineering, market environments, investment decisions, evaluation, and user interfaces. TradeMaster addresses the difficulty of coordinating these components, which can obstruct the use of research methods in real trading workflows.

The platform combines three roles: a software toolkit, an empirical benchmark, and a user interface. These correspond to practical difficulties in building projects, comparing methods, and making systems easier to optimize, maintain, and use. Bringing the roles together aims to support the full research lifecycle rather than a single isolated stage.

The stated objective is infrastructure for transparent, reproducible reinforcement-learning research in trading and support for eventual real-world deployment. The abstract presents this as an open-source platform contribution, with continued development and community participation envisioned. Its significance lies in organizing the engineering and evaluation work needed around learning methods, helping researchers turn separate data sources and algorithms into projects that can be developed and compared systematically.
neurips-2023-trademaster-a-holistic-quan.tldr: TradeMaster combines a toolkit, benchmark, and interface to support reproducible reinforcement-learning research for quantitative trading.

paragraphs: Neural radiance fields reconstruct three-dimensional scenes from photographs, but interactive rendering becomes challenging for large scenes. UE4-NeRF addresses this by combining neural scene representations with the rendering pipeline of Unreal Engine 4. The aim is to make large reconstructed environments render in real time while retaining strong visual quality.

The system divides a large scene into smaller sub-NeRFs. Within the partitions, it initializes polygonal meshes using regular octahedra and optimizes the mesh vertices during training. It also trains meshes with different levels of detail for different observation levels. These representations are combined with UE4's rasterization pipeline to support efficient rendering.

The reported system renders large scenes at 4K resolution with frame rates reaching 43 frames per second. Experiments find rendering quality comparable to state-of-the-art approaches, and working within UE4 also facilitates later scene editing. The contribution is a coordinated representation and rendering design: scene partitioning, optimized meshes, and multiple detail levels make neural reconstructions usable within an established engine for the demonstrated large-scale scenes.
neurips-2023-ue4-nerf-neural-radiance-fi.tldr: UE4-NeRF combines partitioned neural scenes and optimized meshes with Unreal Engine 4 to render large scenes at up to 43 FPS in 4K.
